  "text": "The town hired me to remove names from benches.

Not the plaques. Those stayed. I sanded away the names people scratched into the wood.

“Only the names,” my supervisor said. “Leave the hearts.”

It was easy work until I found my brother’s.

He had been missing for twenty years.

The letters were fresh, pale curls of wood still caught inside the R.

I called my supervisor.

“Common name,” she said.

“His handwriting.”

“Sand it.”

Instead, I sat down.

Someone had carved a heart beside his name. Inside it was tomorrow’s date.

I returned before sunrise with coffee and the pocketknife he’d given me when I was twelve.

At seven, an old woman approached the bench.

“You’re in his place,” she said.

“My brother’s?”

“My husband’s.”

She showed me a photograph. My brother stood beside her, gray-haired, holding a fish.

“He never liked fishing,” I said.

“He learned.”

She touched the carved heart.

“We had forty-three years. Please don’t make him start again.”

Across the park, my supervisor was unlocking the equipment shed.

“How do I bring him home?” I asked.

The woman looked at my knife.

“You give the bench another name.”

I thought of our mother, who still left the porch light on.

Then I opened the blade.

The old woman sat beside me while I worked.

I carved slowly. There was a splinter under my thumbnail, and my hand was shaking.

When I finished, she took my hand.

I knew her then.

“Did you catch anything?” she asked.

“Not today,” I said.

Across the park, a young man stood watching us. He looked so much like my brother that I almost called out."
